newsitem.title: USA: MIA rates little changed, fuel surcharges dropped.
newsitem.headline: MIA rates little changed, fuel surcharges dropped.

text.p: Fuel surcharges to Latin American routes are finally being dropped, but otherwise rates to Latin America from Miami International Airport are little changed, the latest Reuters survey shows.
"All the carriers are dropping them, mostly effective throughout the month of May," one forwarder said.
For example, LanChile and Fast Air dropped their fuel surcharge effective May 5. Fine Air, MIA's largest international freight carrier, dropped its surcharge effective May 15.

The cheaper charges come just as Miami International Airport is entering its summer cargo slowdown. Few perishables are imported because America and Europe can grow their own fruits, vegetables and flowers. MIA's perishable traffic begins to strengthen again in September.
Nonetheless, MIA predicts that the summer will see cargo volumes 5 percent to 8 percent better than last year, according to Peter Reaveley, MIA's manager of route development.
Volumes to Europe continue to be heavy, easing the usual summer slump in rates to Europe. But most expect rates to drop as the holiday charter season picks up.

"We're looking at heavy volumes to Europe this summer, especially to the U.K.," one freight forwarder said. He said he is booking all types of general freight including high tech equipment and auto parts."
Despite the optimism, rates to London have softened slightly, dropping to $1.10, or about a nickel a kilo from last month, the survey shows.
"We have been dealing with the holiday flights since late April and have not yet had to drop rates," one European carrier said.
"We will have to drop rates back, espcially from Orlando, MIA may hold its own," one carrier said. Orlando, because of its many theme park attractions, has more summer charter traffic than Miami.
"We're also starting to see big increases to Asia," a forwarder said. "I don't know if it is related to the sudden increase in lift," he said.

China Airlines began the first direct frighter service to Asia from Miami in mid-March with one weekly Boeing 747 freighter. It added another recently. Rates to Asia are running about $2.25 to $2.50 depending on the destination, freight forwarders said.
"We're getting outstanding service in terms of transit times," one forwarder said.
"This (service) will help MIA keep the Latin-Asian traffic," another freight forwarder said.
As expected, there is less freight moving to Brazil, although forwarders and carriers could not quantify the softening.

"Brazil has slowed down a little with the new regulations," one forwarder said. So far, the slack has not had an effect on rates. In fact, the poll shows a two cents per kilo increase in the last month to $2.05 per kilo to Brazil.
On April 1, Brazil instituted some non-tariff barriers to trade whwn it declared that any consumer goods imported would have to be paid for in cash.

Less trade with Brazil could be a big blow to MIA as latest statistics from Dade County Aviation Department show it is MIA's biggest trading partner with $274 million in goods to and from Brazil passing through MIA in 1995.

"Brazil will start recovering nicely in September," MIA's Reaveley said. Brazil is putting the ownership of many of its telecommunications systems in the hands of investors. This should produce a huge boom in imports of equipment as the new owners upgrade the systems, Reaveley said.

Forwarders are cheering the entry of all-cargo Florida West International Airlines into Peru. Before that, they said with only Arrow Air regularly flying freighters into Peru, rates were high and sometimes lift was hard to obtain.
Although rates to Lima are steady at about $1.15 per kilo, forwarders expect the added competition will push rates down.

MIA's top exports to Peru by weight are computers and peripherals and agricultural and drilling machinery, according to Dade County statistics for 1995. MIA's top imports from Peru by weight are vegetables, clothing and fish.
As predicted earlier, shippers did not enjoy the traditional deeply discounted rates from Miami southbound around the May 12 Mother's Day holiday.
In past years during Valentine's Day and Mother's Day so much extra capacity is added to bring flowers back from Latin America, carriers offer extremely cheap rates to fill the aircraft southbound.
But the rates did not materialize at Valentine's Day and carriers also stood firm for Mother's Day, carriers and forwarders said.
"We would see rates as low as 10 cents a kilo. That is not going to happen again," one forwarder said.
